answer: Geographic variables can serve as either the treatment of interest or a confounder, and the distinction governs whether fixed effects help or harm an analysis. When location itself is the treatment, such as living in an area with cleaner air or better hospital access, county fixed effects absorb the very effect being measured. When location instead proxies for wealth, demographics, or built environment along a back-door path, fixed effects block that path by comparing changes within units over time. There is no universally correct specification; the right choice depends on the causal question and model.

faqs.q: When should I use county fixed effects?
faqs.a: Use fixed effects when geography is a confounder, for example when studying what happens after a county adopts a policy. Comparing the same county before and after blocks back-door paths from stable local characteristics. Avoid them when location is the treatment itself.

faqs.q: How is geography a treatment versus a confounder?
faqs.a: Geography is the treatment when the question is the effect of living somewhere with feature X, such as cleaner air. It is a confounder when location proxies for wealth or demographics that drive both policy adoption and outcomes through a back-door path.

faqs.q: Why can fixed effects absorb a real treatment effect?
faqs.a: If the causal variation you want to study is the place-based difference itself, fixed effects remove all between-place variation, eliminating exactly the contrast that identifies the effect.
